hints.junior: Same three plans, same three prices — reorder them so Enterprise appears first instead of last, and the complaint that Pro at $29 felt expensive mostly disappeared.
hints.mid: Seeing $9 first makes $29 look like more than three times as much; seeing $99 first makes the same $29 look like less than a third — both true, both shaping the same number's perceived expense.
hints.staff: The original research shows this holding up even when people are told an anchor is arbitrary and explicitly told to ignore it — a pricing page's order isn't a neutral formatting choice.

hints.junior: Toggle the two orderings below — same three prices and features in both, only the order changes, notice which plan reads as pricey each time.
hints.mid: The cheapest-first ordering is what most pricing pages ship by default without thinking about it; the priciest-first ordering deliberately sets a high anchor before Pro.
hints.staff: The Most Popular badge stays on the same card, same price, same relative position to the other two in both orderings — only which price anchors the reader first changes.

hints.junior: Anchoring means the first number someone sees becomes the reference point every later number gets judged against, not some absolute sense of what's fair.
hints.mid: Ordering the highest tier first sets a high anchor so a mid-tier price reads as reasonable by comparison; a crossed-out 'original price' does the same thing even when nobody paid it.
hints.staff: Ordering off a real, purchasable option is informative framing; a crossed-out price that was never actually charged is closer to manufacturing a false reference point — the mechanism is identical, the honesty isn't.

hints.junior: If you have a plan you want most people to pick, put a higher-priced option ahead of it in reading order instead of defaulting to plain cheapest-first.
hints.mid: Test tier ordering for real outcomes, fewer 'why is this so expensive' conversations is a measurable result, and watch for a ceiling effect, anchoring shifts perception, it doesn't manufacture willingness to pay from nothing.
hints.staff: Keep reference pricing honest — an anchor from a price never actually charged is a false-reference-price problem in some advertising law, not just a UX nitpick, and it's easy for readers to catch today.

sections.junior: This case is about a pricing page where the exact same middle plan felt expensive in one card order and felt like a good deal in another, with absolutely nothing about the plan itself changed.
sections.mid: The first price someone sees sets a reference point, and every price after it gets judged against that reference rather than against some independent sense of what's fair.
sections.staff: This isn't a trick that only works on inattentive readers, research shows the effect holding up even when people are explicitly warned the anchor number is arbitrary and told to ignore it.

sections.junior: Anchoring means whatever number you see first becomes the yardstick you measure everything after it against, even if that number wasn't meant to be a yardstick at all.
sections.mid: Putting the highest-priced tier first sets a high anchor, so a middle plan that follows reads as comparatively reasonable, that's the exact mechanism behind the ordering.
sections.staff: A real option ordered first is honest framing, but a crossed-out price nobody ever actually paid is manufacturing a reference point that never existed, same mechanism, very different honesty.

sections.junior: Switch between the two orderings and notice which plan your eye judges as the expensive one each time.
sections.mid: All three prices and features are identical in both versions, only the order the cards appear in changes.
sections.staff: The popular badge stays on the same card in both versions, so you can see clearly that only the ordering, not the plan itself, is doing the work here.

sections.junior: The first price a reader sees sets the scale for every price that follows, the same plan can feel expensive or reasonable purely based on what came before it.
sections.mid: Order pricing tiers deliberately, put a higher anchor ahead of the plan you actually want people to choose.
sections.staff: Keep any anchor honest, ordering real purchasable options is legitimate, but a fabricated crossed-out price is a false reference point, not just a UX technique.
